newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - C-TEC's RCN to expand.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - C-TEC's RCN to expand.

text.p: RCN Telecom Services plans to expand into Washington and will need to raise capital to fund its operations as an independent company after the break-up of C-TEC Corp, said C-TEC Chief Executive Officer David McCourt.
McCourt told Reuters in a recent interview that RCN was looking to extend its video, telephone and Internet services to Washington after having established itself in Boston and New York.

C-TEC, based in Princeton, N.J., announced last week that it was splitting in three, dividing its operations along business lines. Its businesses range from cable television to long-distance phone service.
"The move is intended to allow all three operations to focus on the growth of their respective core businesses and to enhance the value of these operations," C-TEC said.
An industry analyst said the plan appeared designed to raise C-TEC's visibility on Wall Street.
"(Wall Street) couldn't figure it out," the analyst said. "It was not really a telephone company, not really a cable company."

McCourt said the three new companies would probably be able to raise capital more easily. "You'll...attract the shareholders you want," he said. "The shareholders that buy into a telephone company are very different from the shareholders that buy into a high-risk, high-growth company like RCN."
McCourt, who will head RCN after the C-TEC split-up, said RCN was considering raising capital for future spending after it becomes independent.
"RCN ...needs to raise a lot of capital and it's going to spend a lot of capital," he said.

RCN, a broadband network company that is changing its name to RCN Corp, is already in talks about entering Washington, he said. "We're working on it," and the company expects to announce a deal soon, he said.
RCN is one of three companies to be created in the break-up of C-TEC at year-end.
RCN operates in Boston and New York as a provider of packaged local and long-distance telephone, video and Internet access services over fibre optic networks.

In September RCN formed a joint venture with Boston Edison Co to offer its services as well as energy management through the utility company's fibre optics networks in Boston and the surrounding area.
RCN has more than 40,000 subscribers in the two cities and revenues totalling more than $4.0 million, McCourt said.
In New York RCN competes with cable provider Time Warner Inc.

The other two companies to result from C-TEC's split-up are CTCo and C-TEC Cable Systems. CTCo will handle local telephone operations and related engineering business in rural Pennsylvania. C-TEC Cable will handle classic cable television operations in Michigan.
McCourt and Peter Kiewit Sons Inc together own 49 percent of C-TEC.
